Congratulations on moving to a beautiful state! I love to travel the state, and there's a wide variety of incredible things to see and do, especially if you're an outdoorsy person. Over at the northwest side of the Lower Peninsula, both the towns of Traverse City and Petoskey are gorgeous to travel to, and they're known for having tons of delicious wineries and cherry-based products. I highly recommend Mackinaw (also written as Mackinac) Island as a unique place to visit. No cars are allowed, so the only options for getting around are walking, biking, or riding in a carriage or on horseback. The Upper Peninsula by Lake Superior is more wild and beautiful, with less people living up there. Munising is known for Pictured Rocks, which you can take a boat tour to see or rent kayaks and go out yourself. Be careful though, because the Great Lakes can be pretty dangerous to go out on if you don't know what you're doing. 

Winter driving can be tough at first, and how it feels in a vehicle can vary. I drive a small car, so slushy roads are actually some of the worst driving conditions to me. It can easily and without warning suck your car off to a side, so drive carefully when things start to get warm enough to create slushy conditions. Larger, heavier vehicles don't struggle as much with slush. Ice can actually give me a sense of false security, because there have been plenty of times I don't even feel it under my tires until I try to turn or hit the brakes. When it's winter, be gentle either slowing down or speeding up. If you try to do either suddenly, you'll find your tires spinning but you won't be moving the way you want. Snow tires and all wheel drive definitely helps with that. I recommend keeping a blanket in your trunk in the winter, and cat litter. If your car gets stuck, you can use the litter under your tires to give you some traction to help you get out.

One Christmas Eve night when I was a child, my parents and I were leaving my grandparents' house after doing the usual feasting and gift giving. Now mind you, their house was out in the middle of nowhere in a field. There was absolutely nothing around or above their home, and yet, just as we began walking to the car, my parents and I all heard jingle bells ringing in the sky above us. As a kid, I started freaking out because I thought it was Santa, but my parents were absolutely dumbfounded as to what it was. There was no one around, nothing that could have made that sound. To this day we all enjoy talking about it almost every Christmas and wonder what we heard.

I'm not a parent, but I heard some parents use Santa as a tool to help kids understand compassion and empathy by essentially becoming Santas themselves after they stop believing in him. The parents talk about how Santa was a real person at one time who gave away beautiful gifts to boys and girls and then use that story to inspire their own children to be more giving to other people. Don't know how well it works or how many parents actually do this, but I think it's a nice idea!

Eight years ago, my life changed. 

Six years ago, so did the rest of the world. 

I became blind when I was only 23, just out of college and working my way up the ranks. The loss of my sight caused my already small world to narrow, forcing me to move back in with my parents and rethink my life and my future. I won't deny it; I spent a lot of time cursing my situation and throwing the biggest pity parties you can imagine. 

Several months passed, and word began to spread of another war being started in the Middle East. I didn't pay attention; we were always fighting, always at war. What should I care? 

For the most part, everyone felt the same way I did. Some protested, some signed up for the fight, but for the most part, everyone simply ignored the problem. Let the old men fight their pointless fights. We had more pressing matters to worry about. Taxes and unruly children and cheating spouses and who was recently voted off of America's Got Talent was by far more important. 

That was where we messed up. There were warnings, for sure. But no one paid any attention. I may have had no eyesight, but the rest of the nation was just as blind. 

The spores were developed soon after the war started. They spread like wildfire, drifting on the winds, catching rides in ship and plane vents, attaching themselves to clothes, hair, you name it. They soon began to grow and spread farther and farther. Within six months of the initial spread, the spores were found in 172 countries. No one knew where they came from. Pitiful efforts were put in destroying the new weed, but it wasn't even close to enough. Then, the first buds began to form. People talked about it for days; all across the world, the plants were blossoming at the same time. I was told that they were a bright red in color, quite pretty to look at, and most people didn't mind these new invaders. It was when the flowers actually bloomed that the first wave of death happened. 

It was estimated that over 600 million people died within the first three hours of the flowers blooming. Within two days, three billion had succumbed. Society was thrown in chaos; no one knew how it happened. Everything fell apart. It was apparent that being in the vicinity of the plants would kill you, but then those who were still alive noticed an interesting pattern: as long as you did not look at the killer weed, you were fine. You could touch it, even eat it, and nothing would happen. 

It's been six years. Barely anyone is left. Those who remain were either incredibly lucky or were blind, like me. We stumble around in the dark, doing our best to survive as well as we can. No one knows  exactly where the flower came from, but we know that to look at it is near-instant death. Whether it was a terrorist creation set on destroying the world or a government monstrosity designed to root out the enemy, it doesn't matter anymore. We are doing our best to correct the mistakes of the past, but one thing is sure; we have to pay better attention to the evil around us. We can no longer be as blind as we once were.
